summary: Remote (off-LAN) live view in the Tapo app for Tapo cameras uses the cloud RELAY path (connection type 0). The app first resolves the CIPC relay-API host with the signed account call /api/v2/common/getAppServiceUrl (serviceIds ['cipc.api.cloud']). It then asks for a relay slot, either over its IoT MQTT session (topic $tpiot/things/<thingName>/relay/request/get, tried first for IoT-cloud cameras) or over HTTPS POST https://<cipcHost>/v2/relay/request with 'Authorization: <account token>' (no 'ut|', no HMAC signing). The response gives relayUrl (host + /relayservice?... path), relayIp, relayToken, optional cdnUrl/activeCert/concurrentType/quicEnable/elbCookie. The app opens TLS (SNI = relay host, chain must verify against TP-Link private roots bundled in e41/b.java) to relayIp:443, sends one never-ending 'POST /relayservice?...&retryTime=N HTTP/1.1' with X-token etc. On '200' the socket becomes a raw tunnel to the camera's /stream multipart session: the client skips the inner HTTP POST /stream + Digest step entirely and directly exchanges the same multipart JSON/MPEG-TS parts as on the LAN :8800 stream. Heartbeat part every 15 s. The app sends nothing to the camera itself; the cloud signals the camera (inferred). Correction to tapo_protocol_spec: ports 17443/18443/19443 belong only to the legacy Kasa-camera path, not Tapo relay.

items.description: Which remote transports exist and how the relay strategy is chosen. Connection types: 256 local, 17 UPnP (public ip:ext_port, TLS-PSK), 16 P2P (STUN/UDT hole punch), 0 relay. For relay the 'middleware' f0 picks RelayStrategy MQTT (default, used when device isSupportIoTCloud and app mqtt enabled) and falls back to CIPC HTTP once MQTT fails; CIPC is retried at most once (counter < 1). A rate-limit blocks a key 'devId_<id>|st_<streamType>|rs_<res>|it_<imgType>' when more than 100 requests per minute.

items.description: Transport to the relay node for concurrentType 'node_https' (HTTP/1.1 class d0, what a Windows client should implement). TCP connect to relayIp (or DNS of relayHost) port 443, TLS via SSLContext 'TLSv1.2', SNI = relayHost, OkHostnameVerifier on relayHost, then the peer chain must verify against one of the TP-Link private roots bundled in e41/b.java. 'node_quic' uses HTTP/3 (xquic) to the same host:443; 'cdn_https'/'cdn_quic' connect to cdnUrl:443 and require the chain to match the roots named in activeCert.

items.description: Handling of the relay node's HTTP response head to the tunnel request.

value.200: tunnel open. Response header 'X-Client-Id' (or 'x-client-id') is stored as rcClientId; header 'pre_connection: 1' marks a pre-connection. Start 15 s heartbeat timer. All further bytes are tunnel payload.
value.304: redirect: body is a RequestUrlResult JSON; take relayIp, relayToken and relayUrl (host / path split) and reconnect (X-Redirect-Times increments).
value.other: body is HttpResult JSON {errorCode,msg,result}; errorCode stored as failure reason. errorCode -33 resets/marks the device data-timeout counter.
value.relay_errors_in_stream: relay-level failures are surfaced to the player as a JSON part {type:'error', ... error_code} (code -11002 for transport failures)

items.description: What flows inside the tunnel after the 200. The app bridges the tunnel to a loopback ServerSocketChannel (bind port 0) and its normal stream client (tb1.a) connects there over plain TCP. For connection type 0 the stream client does NOT send the inner 'POST /stream' request and does NOT run Digest: tb1.a.s(auth, true) just sets code 204. So no Key-Exchange header is received and no AES key is derived (cipher stays null). The client immediately writes multipart JSON control parts (same format as LAN :8800, boundary '----client-stream-boundary--') e.g. the preview request, and reads device parts (boundary '----device-stream-boundary--') carrying JSON responses and MPEG-TS media exactly like the LAN stream.

value.media_encryption: no Key-Exchange => parts are returned as-is; if a part had X-If-Encrypt: 1 with no cipher the bytes pass through undecrypted. Treat relay media as plaintext MPEG-TS inside the TLS tunnel.
value.session_id: X-Session-Id header from the preview response is reused on later control parts, as on LAN

items.description: How the camera learns about the relay session. The app sends no passthrough/services-sync call to the camera for relay; its only requests are getAppServiceUrl, /v2/relay/request (or the MQTT relay/request/get publish) and the tunnel POST. The relay request carries deviceId + streamType + resolution + trackId, so the cloud relay service must notify the camera over the camera's own persistent cloud connection and the camera dials the same relay node. The client never needs the camera's LAN IP, the localAccessToken or Digest for relay.

items.description: P2P path (type 16), recorded only at summary depth. The app runs STUN (stun.tplinkcloud.com, port 3478; beta: stun-beta.tplinkcloud.com) to learn its NAT mapping, asks the camera through the cloud to punch with a 'p2p' request, then runs UDT over UDP and a secureV4 key schedule from appNonce/devNonce (see tapo_protocol_spec stream.local8800.encryption.secure_v4_p2p). Not recommended for a first Windows implementation.
End-to-end recipe for a Windows client to show remote live view, using only the CIPC + node_https path.

steps: 1. TP-Link ID login (existing cloud.* items) -> account token T, appServerUrl, terminal uuid U.
2. Device list -> camera deviceId D, deviceType, isSupportIoTCloud (cloudType 2/1).
3. Signed POST {appServerUrl}/api/v2/common/getAppServiceUrl body {"serviceIds":["cipc.api.cloud"]} -> H = serviceUrls['cipc.api.cloud'] (strip scheme). Cache it.

4. POST https://H/v2/relay/request, headers Authorization: T, User-Agent: Tapo_APP/<model>/3.22.806_Android/Android <ver>, X-Request-Signature: <10 random alnum>, X-Client-Id: U, X-Source: tapo-app, X-Brand: TPLINK, X-Ca-Type: cloud-self, Content-Type: application/json; charset=UTF-8; body {deviceId:D, dataTimeoutCount:0, cloudType, deviceType, playerId:U, rootCaVer:'1', preConnection:0, resolution:'HD'|'VGA', streamType:0, customParams:'{}', trackId:<uuid>}.
5. If errorCode -1102: re-login and retry once. Else take relayUrl -> relayHost + relayPath, relayIp, relayToken, elbCookie.
6. TCP connect relayIp (or DNS relayHost):443, TLS with SNI relayHost, verify host name and chain against TP-Link roots from e41/b.java.

7. Write 'POST <relayPath>&retryTime=0 HTTP/1.1' + headers of remote.relay.tunnel.request (X-token: relayToken, X-Pull-Mode: 2, X-Version: 2.0, Keep-Relay: 3600, Content-Type multipart boundary, huge Content-Length) + blank line.
8. Read response head. 304 -> parse body as RequestUrlResult and reconnect; non-200 -> parse {errorCode} and fail.
9. On 200: write the preview request JSON part (stream.control.preview) directly; no inner POST /stream, no Digest.
10. Parse device multipart parts as on LAN; media parts are MPEG-TS (expected plaintext); send heartbeat part every 15 s; send stop request ({method:'do',stop:'null'}) before closing.

unresolved.detail: No Key-Exchange is received on the relay path, so the app derives no AES key. Whether the camera ever sets X-If-Encrypt: 1 on relay parts (and with what key) must be checked with a live capture. If it does, check the HKDF/MD5 schemes with the account password as for LAN.
No expiry field besides preConnIdleTime; the app requests a fresh relay slot for every connection. Assume a single use.
Server-side behaviour (relay time limit 'TAPO_RELAY_LIMIT', -100001 RELAY_REQUEST_LIMIT, daily remote-view quota) is enforced in the cloud and not visible in the APK.
